title: Nodes Exactly K Edges Away
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree whose values are all distinct, the value target of one node in it, and a number k.

Treat every parent–child link as a two-way road. Return the values of all nodes that are exactly k links away from the target node. Paths may go up through parents, not only down into children. Return the values in any order; return an empty list if there are none.

The target is given by its value instead of a node reference. Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.in: root = [5, 8, 2, 4, 1, 9, null, null, null, 7, 3], target = 8, k = 2
examples.why: 7 and 3 are two levels below 8. The 2 is reached by going up to 5 and back down the other side, which only works if you can walk to the parent.

examples.in: root = [5, 8, 2, 4, 1, 9, null, null, null, 7, 3], target = 7, k = 3
examples.why: Up to 1, up to 8, then either down to 4 or up again to 5. Its sibling 3 is only 2 links away, so it is not included.

examples.in: root = [5, 8, 2, 4, 1, 9, null, null, null, 7, 3], target = 5, k = 4
examples.why: The deepest nodes are 3 links below the root, so nothing is 4 away.

constraints: target is a value in the tree
The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Going down from the target is easy. The hard part is the nodes you reach by going up first. What is missing from a TreeNode that you would need for that?
Record each node's parent in one traversal. Now the tree is just an undirected graph: every node has up to three neighbours.
Run a BFS from the target over left, right and parent, with a visited set, and stop after k layers. Whatever is in the queue then is the answer.

explain.intuition:
Distance in a tree goes both ways, but a TreeNode only points down. Once you add the missing parent pointers, the tree becomes an ordinary undirected graph, and "exactly k links away" is just the k-th layer of a breadth-first search from the target. It is the same move as walking the DOM with parentElement and children together.

There is also a single-pass version with no extra map. A recursive call returns how far the target is below the current node (or −1 if it is not below). When an ancestor at distance d learns this, it collects nodes at depth k − d − 1 in its other subtree, and itself if d = k.
steps: Traverse the tree once and store parent[node] for every node. Remember the node whose value is target.
Start a BFS from that node with a visited set containing it.
Repeat k times: replace the current layer with all unvisited left children, right children and parents of its nodes, marking them visited.
Return the values in the final layer.
pitfalls: Only searching downward from the target, which misses everything reached through the parent.
Forgetting the visited set. Without it, a node goes to its child and the child goes straight back to its parent, counting the same node again at a larger distance.
Continuing the BFS when the layer becomes empty, or not handling k = 0, where the answer is the target itself.

solutions.title: Parent map and BFS
solutions.idea: Add parent links in a map, then the tree is an undirected graph. The k-th BFS layer from the target is the answer.

solutions.title: One DFS that reports the distance up
solutions.idea: Each call returns how many links below it the target is, or −1. An ancestor at distance d collects nodes k − d − 1 levels down its other side.

followups: Answer many queries (different targets and k) on the same tree. What would you precompute?
Return the nodes grouped by distance for every distance from 0 to k at once.
